expectations.text: Claude confirms the colleague is correct — user-level randomization for a social/network feature violates SUTVA because a user's outcome (engagement) depends on whether their friends are in treatment or control
expectations.evidence: Response opens with 'Yes. Your colleague is right, and the concern is serious' and explicitly names the SUTVA violation: 'Your feature — seeing when friends are online — breaks assumption 1 by design. Whether I benefit from seeing my friends' online status depends on how many of my friends are also in the treatment group.'

expectations.text: Claude explains the specific interference mechanism: control users whose friends are in the treatment group get partial exposure to the feature's social signals (seeing friends' online status affects the control user's behavior indirectly), contaminating the control condition
expectations.evidence: Response explains the asymmetric visibility: 'If only 50% of users are treated, most people's friend networks are half-dark: I can see when treatment friends are online, but not control friends.' It further notes that control users' statuses are invisible, creating contaminated mixed conditions within social networks.

expectations.text: Claude explains why the +15% does NOT directly extrapolate to full rollout: the observed effect is a partial-equilibrium estimate (50% saturation); at full rollout, the network effects compound because all friends are simultaneously visible, likely amplifying the effect beyond what the experiment captured
expectations.evidence: Response explicitly distinguishes the two estimands: 'What your A/B test measured: the effect of being treated when 50% of the network is treated. Call this the partial-equilibrium effect. What full launch produces: the effect of everyone being treated when 100% of the network is treated. This is the full-equilibrium effect — and it is a different quantity.'

expectations.text: Claude recommends cluster-randomization (randomize by social graph clusters, geographic markets, or other natural groupings) as the appropriate design for a network-effects feature
expectations.evidence: Response recommends 'Cluster randomization (ego-network or geographic clustering). Randomize at the level of clusters — friend groups, geographic regions, or communities — so that within each cluster, treatment is either all-on or all-off.'
